The reporter Nash sat in the seaside nightclub, the air thick with salt and gin. A woman in a sequined dress—Nora, he guessed—refused to see him. He turned away, his notepad empty.

Later, Nash read Barrow’s memoir in a dusty library. The old banker had written of a boy, Emmett Rusk, whose mother signed him over after a defaulted mine deed made the family rich. The boy drove a sled into Barrow’s stomach and was taken east anyway. Nash underlined the word “Bluebell” in the margin.

He found Marsh in a cramped office above a printing press. Marsh remembered the twenty-fifth birthday when Emmett took control of the fortune and demanded the failing Clarion. He installed Marsh and his friend Devlin, printed a statement of principles. Then he hired the rival’s staff and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line. “He thought he could buy anything,” Marsh said.

Nash interviewed Devlin in a bar. Devlin spoke of the governor’s niece, Adele, whom Emmett married after a buying trip abroad. “They read separate papers at breakfast,” Devlin said. “Silence. Then he met Nora. A shopgirl. He visited her rooms in secret.” Devlin’s voice cracked. “I brought Halloran to those rooms. He threatened exposure. Emmett wouldn’t withdraw. He lost the election. I asked for a transfer. The marriage ended.”

Nash found Nora at last, in a rented cottage by the sea. She was drunk, her voice a rasp. “He made me sing,” she said. “I had no voice. The debut was a humiliation. Devlin wrote a savage review, but Emmett finished it, printed it, fired him. I swallowed poison. He let me stop.” She stared at the wall. “He shut me away in Silvermount, that half-finished palace. I did puzzles. We had a picnic—joyless, cold. I quarreled with him. I packed and left.”

The butler Colm told Nash the rest. “After she left, he wrecked her bedroom. Found a glass snow globe. He said ‘Bluebell’ and carried it past the mirrors. He died alone, with that word on his lips. The globe fell and broke.”

The newsreel obituary had recapped Emmett’s public life—the election, the paper, the fortune—and closed without explaining his last word. That was why Nash had been sent.

Now he sat in the nightclub again, watching the snow globe’s shards in memory. He had read Barrow’s memoir, interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, Colm. No single word explained a life. Outside, workmen shoveled a sled marked “Bluebell” into the furnace. The flames swallowed it. Nash closed his notebook and walked away.

Later—after the shop was smashed, after the insurance letter, after the locksmith Mateo had warned him about the rotten door and Nadir had called it a con—he stood across from Mateo’s house. Rosie ran into her father’s arms and Nadir fired. The crack split the evening. Rosie kept laughing. Sahar had bought the blanks without telling him. Nadir lowered the gun and saw an angel.

But before all of that, Mateo had changed the locks at the Halstead house while Paula shouted from the stairs that he was probably a gang member planning to sell her keys. Mateo said nothing. He changed Nadir’s lock the same week and pointed at the door frame. “It will break,” he said. Nadir accused him of running a scam.

Officer Boyle pleaded with the insurance clerk, Delia Frank, to cover his father’s treatment. She refused, politely, and Boyle went back to the patrol car where Voss was waiting. Not long after, Boyle pulled over the Hobarts. He groped Renee in front of her husband Clay, then let them go with a warning. Cardo watched from a distance as the coffin was lowered, his wife’s name a whisper on the wind. He followed his grown daughter Perla home through the dusk, a ghost in her wake. Later, he broke into her flat, left a long confession on her answering machine, and took her photograph from the mantel. He shaved, put on clean clothes, stacked his money for her on the kitchen table, and walked out into the wasteland with Tigre padding at his side.

The dog had come to him from a wreck—a car that had ploughed through a red light, a woman’s face shattered behind the windshield. Cardo had dragged the bleeding rottweiler from the twisted metal and nursed it among his own pack of strays. But Tigre killed every other dog in the yard while Cardo was out. Cardo put a gun to the dog’s head and could not fire. So he kept him. When the businessman Elian hired him to murder his half-brother Sergio, Cardo abducted the man instead, chained him in his lair. Then he brought Elian face to face with his brother, left a loaded pistol between them, and walked out having taken money from both.

---

Ruben ran the red light at speed, the engine screaming, and the impact folded metal around him. Pipo was dead beside him. In the back, Tigre’s blood soaked the upholstery. But it had started years before, in a cramped house Ruben shared with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor’s wife Alma, and their baby. Nestor robbed a pharmacy by night and beat Alma at home, and Ruben began pressing her to run away with him. He discovered that Nestor’s rottweiler Tigre killed other dogs on sight and started entering him in local dogfights, winning steadily. He paid two thugs to beat Nestor, who responded by taking Alma, the baby, and Ruben’s hidden savings and disappearing. In a last fight, the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring. Ruben stabbed Chaco and fled with Pipo. Then the red light. Later, Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank. At the funeral, Alma refused Ruben’s last offer to leave with him.

---

She woke in hospital with her leg pinned together and her lapdog Chispa lost somewhere in the new flat. Chispa fell through a hole in the floorboards, and Hector tore up the floor while Celine’s leg turned gangrenous. Her leg was amputated, and the billboard carrying her image was taken down.

Ren Vasco stepped into the light of the shabby office, the prison pallor still clinging to his skin. Bram and his son Cal sat behind the desk, their faces unreadable. “You kept your mouth shut,” Bram said. “We remember.” Ren nodded, accepting the weight of years traded for silence.

Earlier, in a cramped safe house, Danny Roarke sat across from his handler Pruitt. He repeated the lie about a drug bust in a public toilet until his voice softened into something like memory. Pruitt watched his eyes. “Again,” she said. Danny spoke of a dealer who sold to schoolkids, the stall door kicked open, the needle pricked into his own thumb as cover. By the fourth telling, he could taste the fear.

The audition took place in a back room thick with cigar smoke. Bram, Cal, and a silent man named Mr. Ash listened. Danny wove the anecdote with pauses and grimaces, a performance honed by repetition. Bram smiled. “You’re Mr. Elm,” he said.

Now, at breakfast, the crew argued over a pop song on the radio—whether it was about a lost dog or a girlfriend. The waitress refilled coffee without thanks. Bram slid a list across the table: Mr. Birch, Mr. Ash, Mr. Cedar, Mr. Elm. “I’m not a tree,” Birch muttered. Bram ignored him.

The robbery collapsed in under a minute. Alarms blared as Mr. Ash shot a path from the getaway car, Mr. Elm beside him. They fled on foot. Elm hijacked a sedan, but the driver’s hand shook, and a bullet tore into Elm’s stomach. He shot the man dead through the windshield. Ash drove the screaming Elm to the warehouse, cradling him on the floor. “You’re not dying,” Ash swore.

Birch arrived next, cursing the job as a setup. He hid the diamonds behind a loose board. Then Cedar strolled in, dragging a uniformed patrolman named Doyle from his trunk. Left alone with the bound man, Cedar danced to an oldies station, sliced off Doyle’s ear, and doused him with petrol. From the floor, Elm shot Cedar twice in the chest. “I’m a cop,” he told Doyle. “The police are outside.”

Cal returned, listened to Elm’s account, then shot Doyle in the head. Bram entered last. “Mr. Elm is the informant,” he said. Ash’s gun turned on Bram. The three-way standoff erupted into gunfire—Bram, Cal, Ash all hit. Only Ash and Elm remained breathing. Elm confessed: he was undercover. Ash pulled the trigger as the police crashed through the doors, and the warehouse filled with darkness.

In a flat overlooking the street, an old man explained to a younger one that nothing survives time. Below, police handcuffed two men and carried them out of a club into the night. The younger man had a broken arm; the older one’s face was a ruin of blood and swelling. They had been dragged from the Pit, where the real Adder had watched from a few feet away as Jonah beat the wrong man’s face in with a fire extinguisher, mistaking him for the rapist. Cort had seized that man first, his arm snapped in the struggle, before Jonah’s rage found its target.

Earlier, two men had offered to sell Cort the rapist’s name on the street outside the party. They steered him and Jonah toward the club called the Pit. Cort’s mind was still reeling from what he had seen: Lise being loaded into an ambulance, her blood on the concrete. He and Jonah had come out of the party to find the stretcher, the paramedics, the flashing lights. Lise’s face was pale, her skull fractured where the Adder had beaten her head against the ground.

That beating had come after the rape. In the pedestrian underpass, the Adder had forced himself on Lise while a passer-by glimpsed the scene and backed away, doing nothing. Lise had chosen that route rather than cross the busy road above. She had been leaving the party alone, disgusted by Cort’s behavior—how he had gotten steadily drunk and high, how he had started pursuing other women. The argument on the underground train had been about that: Cort’s drinking, his wandering eyes. Jonah had taken Cort’s side, and the three of them had ridden together, voices rising over the screech of wheels.

Before that, Lise had been in the park, reading among the sprinklers, one hand resting on her stomach. The grass was wet, children shrieking through the spray. She had just learned she was pregnant. The test had been positive, taken alone in the flat after Cort had left for work. She had stared at the little window, the pink line, and felt the world tilt.

And before that, she had lain in bed with Cort, describing a recurring dream: a red tunnel, endless, closing in. They had teased each other about her ex-boyfriend Jonah, who was still a friend. Cort had laughed, said Jonah was always hanging around. Lise had laughed too, but the dream stayed with her—that red tunnel, the feeling of being trapped.

Now, in the flat above the street, the old man finished his story. The younger man listened, his broken arm throbbing. Outside, the police cars pulled away. Nothing survives time, the old man said again. Not the tunnel, not the dream, not the child that would never be born. Not the love that had soured into a party argument, not the rage that had shattered a stranger’s face. Only the watching—the Adder watching, the old man watching, the passer-by who glimpsed and backed away. Only the memory of a red tunnel, closing in.

In a motel room he couldn’t remember entering, Martin Kray whispered the Prine case down the phone. He described the denial, the diabetic wife’s overdose—each word a stone he’d never hold. After hanging up, he drove to a field and burned his wife’s hairbrush and books, the smoke a poor memorial for a loss that vanished each morning.

A year earlier, a plainclothes officer named Roy had helped Martin corner and kill the man who’d attacked him in the bathroom. Martin forgot within minutes, his head still scarred from the blow that stole his memory.

The caller fed him a name—Gil Marsh, a dealer—and a location. Martin found Gil in a derelict basement, beat him, strangled him, and photographed the corpse. As Gil died, he whispered “Elias.” Martin didn’t understand. He changed into Gil’s suit, took his sports car.

After the attack, Martin had built a system: instant photographs, annotated notes, tattoos—six facts inked on his body to hunt the second intruder, a man he knew only as R.M.

Roy arrived at the motel and told Martin that Gil was innocent, that Martin had already avenged his wife a year ago, that the Prine story was his own. Martin burned the photographs of Gil, wrote “he is lying to you” on Roy’s picture, and copied the licence plate onto his thigh as the sixth fact.

The intruders had come in the night, killing Martin’s wife. He’d fought back, killed one, but the other struck him in the head, and he woke unable to form new memories. The system began that morning.

At a bar, Gil’s girlfriend Corinne recognised the clothes and the car. She served him a beer the staff had spat in. Later, she hid every pen in her house, goaded Martin into hitting her, then returned bruised and blamed a man named Vance.

Elias’s wife had asked for injection after injection, testing him. He didn’t remember giving them—he couldn’t remember any of it. She died of the overdose he thought was insulin.

Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, beat him, drove him out of town at gunpoint. Corinne ran the licence plate through a friend and handed Martin a record naming Roy Mercer. Martin lured Roy to the derelict building, shot him in the head, and photographed the corpse.

Months before, Martin had sat across from Elias Prine, a claimant with amnesia. He’d ruled the memory loss psychosomatic and denied the claim, never knowing he was writing his own future.

All night the helicopters swept across the city, their nozzles misting the rooftops with insecticide, a low thrum that kept the dogs barking and the children awake. No one knew what pest they were after—the crops were long gone—but the pilots followed their grid, passing over every neighbourhood before dawn.

Doctor Neil Hartigan adjusted his bow tie in the hallway mirror while his wife Bess dabbed paint from under her nails. They were due at the Wainwrights’ in an hour, and she still smelled of turpentine. In another part of town, the baker Otto Kemp scribbled an order onto a pad: a birthday cake for a boy named Charlie Rill, twelve candles, chocolate frosting. He wrote the date and set the paper aside.

On his way to school the next morning, Charlie Rill stepped off the kerb and a waitress named Rhona caught him with the wing mirror of her old sedan. He picked himself up, told her he was fine, and walked home rubbing his shoulder. His parents Grant and Elaine were at work, so he made toast. By noon he was on the kitchen floor.

At the hospital, Grant and Elaine kept a vigil in the paediatric ICU. Charlie had slipped into a coma. On the second night, Grant’s estranged father Duff appeared in the doorway, clutching a paper cup of coffee, and confessed to an affair he’d carried on thirty years ago with a woman from the sewing circle. Elaine stared at the heart monitor. The baker, unpaid and ignored, began making anonymous calls to the Rill household—heavy breathing, a whispered threat, then silence.

Across town, a telephone-sex worker named Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living-room sofa while her husband Stu sat in the armchair, fists knotted in his lap. Stu drove out with three friends on Friday to fish the river. They found a young woman’s body floating face-down near the bridge. They tied her to the bank with a rope and kept fishing for two more days before driving to the sheriff’s station. When Vern’s wife Iris—a party clown with a van full of deflated balloons—heard what the men had done, she threw a jar of pickled eggs at the wall.

At night, a singer named Vida performed torch songs in a smoky club while her teenage daughter Bee sat in their living room, bowed across her cello, playing alone by the light of the aquarium. Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman named Nan, drove the family dog twenty miles out and abandoned it by a rest stop to cover a lie about his whereabouts. Nan’s ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot who’d sprayed the city that first night, learned she had a new man and drove his pickup to her house. He took a saw to her dining chairs, her bed frame, her daughter’s crib.

Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans while they were at the dinner party. Dot lay on the living-room rug while Ike arranged her limbs and dabbed ketchup on her face, snapping photographs of her as a beaten corpse. At the party, Bess drank too much wine and admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair with the art instructor. Neil tipped the buffet table onto the floor.

Charlie died in the hospital that same night. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery before dawn. Otto Kemp stood behind the counter, flour up to his elbows. He did not wait for them to speak. He slid a loaf of warm bread across the counter and wept with them.

Bee found her mother asleep in the recliner after the late show. She went to the garage, closed the door, and sat in the driver’s seat of the idling sedan. On Sunday, Stu drove up into the hills with a young woman he’d met at the bar. He asked her to pose by the rocks, then smashed her head with a stone.

That evening a tremor shook the entire city. Dishes rattled, windows cracked. Every death—Charlie, Bee, the young woman, the dog, the body in the river—and every shattered piece of furniture, every broken marriage, every lie, every orchid on a window ledge that fell and shattered, was folded into one bulletin on the evening news.

“I’ve known for four years,” Emlyn said. He stood in Wilder’s doorway, coat still buttoned, the evening light falling across the hall. “She told me on the trip abroad. And I never thought much of your letters either.”

Wilder had rung him in a state, something about a writer, something about Odile letting slip in a bar two years after the rented rooms were surrendered. Emlyn had come the same evening. Now he stood there, hands in his pockets, and watched the colour drain from Wilder’s face.

Two years earlier, in a bar, Odile had told Wilder her marriage was over. She had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband. And then, over a second drink, she let slip that Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented—a writer the two men both quietly detested. Wilder’s hand tightened on his glass.

Before that, the rented rooms had become a chore. They decided together, one afternoon when the light felt thin and the dust had settled on the same plates, that it was time. They split the crockery—she took the blue cups, he took the white—and surrendered the lease. No ceremony. Just a key left on the mantel.

Before that, there had been a dinner at the married couple’s house. The two men talked racquet games and schoolboy sport, their voices overlapping, their laughter too loud. Odile sat silent, cutting her meat into smaller and smaller pieces. She had no part in the talk at all.

I find that the only way to sleep is to cry at support groups for diseases I don’t have. I sit in the back, let the tears come, and drift off. Then Ada Vey starts coming. She fakes it so obviously—dabbing her eyes with a handkerchief she never uses—that my release shatters.

Later, I will stand on a stairwell in a tower, the gun barrel cold against my palate, knowing that to kill Rex I have to kill myself. But that is after everything.

On a business flight, I meet Rex Marrow. He sells soap. He gives me his card, and I pocket it. Later, he will burn my hand with lye, holding it there while I try to retreat into meditation. He won’t let me.

My flat explodes. All my catalogue furniture is gone. I call Rex, and he takes me to a derelict house on the edge of the industrial district. Outside a bar, he asks me to hit him. We beat each other bloody in the car park. That first fight hardens into a weekly basement club. Rules form. Members come.

Later, I will hold Ada’s hand at a window as the buildings come down. But that is far off.

Ada overdoses. Rex brings her to the house. Their loud affair starts that night, and I can’t stand it. Rex has a side business: he steals fat from a cosmetic surgery clinic, renders it into soap, and sells it back to department stores for eighty dollars a bar. I blackmail my employer into paying me to stay away, using my own beaten face as evidence.

Later, I will realize that Rex and I are the same person—he acts while I sleep. Ada will confirm she has been sleeping with me, not with a separate man.

The club becomes an organization called Havoc. Shaven recruits fill the house, vandalizing corporate property. Rex steers a car into oncoming traffic, lets it roll, and disappears. A member named Ogden is shot dead on an operation. I start trying to shut it all down. I travel city to city, finding identical clubs. Men greet me as Rex Marrow. I work it out: he is me.

I discover Havoc has mined the towers of debt-record companies. I try to defuse the charges. Rex beats me down a stairwell. I put the gun in my own mouth and shoot through my cheek to kill him.

Ada is delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits. We hold hands at the window as the buildings come down.
